sets.title: Digestive physiology and metabolism past questions

questions.stem: The term 'metabolism':

options.label: A
options.text: refers to all the chemical reactions that occur in the body

options.label: B
options.text: includes the synthesis of complex molecules from simpler ones

options.label: C
options.text: includes the breakdown of complex molecules into simpler ones

questions.why: Metabolism covers the body's chemical reactions. Anabolic pathways build larger molecules, whereas catabolic pathways break down molecules and can release usable energy.

notes.A: This is the overall definition of metabolism and includes pathways in every tissue.
notes.B: Building complex molecules from smaller precursors is anabolism, one part of metabolism.
notes.C: Breaking complex molecules into smaller products is catabolism, the other broad part of metabolism.
notes.D: Both anabolic and catabolic pathways are included, often with intermediates linking the two.

questions.stem: An example of absorption is the:

options.label: B
options.text: active transport of glucose into a villus

options.label: C
options.text: hydrolysis of a peptide into amino acids

options.label: D
options.text: release of secretin in the presence of HCl

questions.why: Intestinal absorption transfers digested material across the mucosa. At the brush border, SGLT1 uses the sodium gradient to take glucose into an enterocyte. Glucose then leaves across the basolateral membrane and reaches villus capillaries.

notes.A: Peristalsis moves material along the lumen. This is propulsion and involves no transfer across the epithelium.
notes.C: Peptide hydrolysis is chemical digestion. It supplies amino acids that can subsequently be absorbed.
notes.D: Duodenal acid stimulates S cells to release secretin. This is endocrine signalling in response to luminal contents.
notes.E: Peptide hydrolysis is digestion, while secretin release is endocrine secretion. Both can precede absorption.

questions.stem: Chewing food aids digestion by:

options.label: B
options.text: increasing the surface area of the food

options.label: C
options.text: breaking up large protein molecules into peptides

questions.why: Chewing physically fragments food. The smaller pieces have more exposed surface area for digestive enzymes, and mixing with saliva moistens the bolus for swallowing.

notes.A: Fat and amino acids in the duodenum stimulate CCK release, which contracts the gallbladder. Chewing aids digestion directly by fragmenting food.
notes.C: Hydrolysis of peptide bonds requires proteases such as pepsin, which acts in the stomach.
notes.D: Salivary amylase hydrolyses starch while the food is being chewed. That chemical reaction is due to the enzyme.
notes.E: Lingual and gastric lipases can hydrolyse some triglyceride. The teeth break up food particles without hydrolysing lipid molecules.

questions.stem: A function of the small intestine is to:
questions.why: The small intestine is the main site of nutrient uptake. Villi and brush-border microvilli enlarge the absorptive surface. Most water-soluble nutrients enter villus capillaries, while chylomicrons first enter the lacteals.

notes.A: Hepatocytes produce bile. The small intestine receives bile through the bile duct and uses its bile salts during lipid digestion.
notes.B: Blood filtration and removal of many soluble wastes are functions of the kidneys.
notes.C: Some vitamins are made by intestinal bacteria, especially in the colon. The small-intestinal epithelium is specialised for nutrient uptake.
notes.E: Hydrochloric acid is secreted by gastric parietal cells. Bicarbonate helps neutralise that acid when chyme reaches the duodenum.

questions.stem: In the GI tract, the layer, responsible for absorption and secretion is:
questions.why: The mucosa lines the gut lumen. Its epithelium contains absorptive cells and secretory cells, and its glands contribute secretions suited to each segment of the tract.

notes.B: The submucosa contains vessels, lymphatics and a nerve plexus. Some regions have submucosal glands, but the surface epithelium performs most absorption.
notes.C: The muscularis externa contains smooth muscle layers that mix and propel the contents.
notes.D: The serosa is an outer mesothelial covering that reduces friction where the gut is covered by peritoneum.
notes.E: The adventitia is external connective tissue that anchors parts of the gut to surrounding structures.

questions.stem: Most of the chemical and mechanical digestion is carried out within:
questions.why: The small intestine is the principal site of digestion overall. Segmentation mixes chyme with bile and pancreatic juice, and pancreatic and brush-border enzymes complete most chemical digestion. The stomach also provides substantial mechanical mixing.

notes.A: The pylorus regulates the passage of chyme into the duodenum. Antral grinding helps reduce particle size before emptying.
notes.B: The gastric fundus is a reservoir that accommodates a meal. Much of the vigorous gastric grinding takes place farther distally.
notes.C: The stomach churns food and starts substantial protein digestion, but most enzymatic breakdown of the meal is completed downstream.
notes.D: The large intestine absorbs water and electrolytes and supports bacterial fermentation of residual substrates. It receives chyme after most digestion has occurred.

questions.stem: The chyme movement and flow into the stomach is controlled by:

options.label: E
options.text: both the nervous system and various digestive system hormones

questions.why: Gastric motility is regulated by both the enteric nervous system (parasympathetic/sympathetic) and hormones (gastrin, secretin, CCK).

notes.A: True, but hormones too.
notes.B: Not a controller.
notes.C: True, but nerves too.
notes.D: Not a controller.

questions.stem: Gastrointestinal hormones:

options.label: A
options.text: are secreted by exocrine glands of the gut mucosa and affect metabolism

options.label: B
options.text: are secreted into the blood stream by specialized cells in the gut walls and modulate its motor and secretory activity

options.label: C
options.text: are secreted by the gastric walls and protect the gut mucosa from the effect of HCl and proteolytic enzymes

options.label: D
options.text: are situated in the epithelial intestinal cells (enterocytes) and control the cell metabolism of nutrients

options.label: E
options.text: are secreted by the gastric walls and colon and protect the gut mucosa from the effect of HCl and proteolytic and nucleic enzymes

questions.why: Specialised enteroendocrine cells release hormones across the basolateral membrane. Circulating hormones such as gastrin and cholecystokinin alter digestive secretion or motility at their target tissues.

notes.A: Exocrine glands release products into the lumen via ducts or epithelial surfaces. Endocrine release delivers a signal to the circulation.
notes.C: The stomach produces hormones such as gastrin, but its immediate protection from acid and pepsin depends heavily on the mucus and bicarbonate barrier.
notes.D: Enterocytes are chiefly absorptive cells. Specialised enteroendocrine cells provide the principal endocrine signals from the gut epithelium.
notes.E: Mucosal protection depends on epithelial barriers and protective secretions. Digestive hormones act as regulatory signals from multiple gut regions.

questions.stem: The gastrointestinal enzymes:

options.label: A
options.text: are situated in the epithelial intestinal cells (enterocytes) and control cell metabolism

options.label: B
options.text: are secreted into the blood stream by specialized cells in the gut walls and modulate its motor and secretory activity

options.label: C
options.text: are secreted by exocrine glands of the gut mucosa and break down nutrients

options.label: D
options.text: are secreted by the gastric walls and protect the gut mucosa from the effect of HCl and proteolytic enzymes

options.label: E
options.text: are secreted by the gastric walls into the small intestine and protect the gut mucosa from the effect of HCl, proteolytic and nucleic enzymes

questions.why: Digestive enzymes are exocrine secretions that break down macromolecules into absorbable units.

notes.A: Not GI enzymes.
notes.B: Hormones.
notes.D: Mucus.
notes.E: Mucus.

questions.stem: All are GIT hormones except:
questions.why: Erythropoietin is produced mainly by renal interstitial cells in adults in response to hypoxia. It stimulates red cell production in bone marrow. The other options are signalling peptides produced in the gut.

notes.A: Cholecystokinin is secreted by small-intestinal I cells and promotes gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion.
notes.B: Gastrin is released from G cells, chiefly in the gastric antrum, and stimulates acid secretion.
notes.C: Secretin comes from duodenal S cells in response to acid and increases bicarbonate secretion by the pancreas.
notes.E: Somatostatin from gastric and intestinal D cells acts locally and can inhibit gastrin and other digestive secretions.

questions.stem: The enzyme amylase is secreted by:
questions.why: Salivary glands secrete alpha-amylase into the mouth, and pancreatic acinar cells secrete it into pancreatic juice. Both enzymes hydrolyse internal alpha-1,4 linkages in starch.

notes.A: The liver produces bile, and the duodenum receives pancreatic amylase. Neither is a major source of digestive alpha-amylase.
notes.B: Pancreatic acini produce amylase. The duodenum is the site where that enzyme is delivered and acts.
notes.C: Salivary glands produce amylase, but the liver contributes bile rather than the second major supply of digestive amylase.
notes.E: The stomach secretes pepsinogen, and the duodenum receives amylase from the pancreas. Salivary amylase can act briefly after swallowing.

questions.stem: The digestive enzyme, produced in the salivary glands and the pancreas is:
questions.why: Alpha-amylase is secreted into saliva and pancreatic juice. It hydrolyses starch to smaller carbohydrates, which brush-border enzymes then convert to absorbable monosaccharides.

notes.A: Maltase activity is present in the intestinal brush border and releases glucose from maltose.
notes.C: Chief cells in the stomach secrete pepsinogen, which becomes pepsin in the acidic gastric lumen.
notes.D: Pancreatic nucleases are delivered to the small intestine to digest nucleic acids. They are not the digestive enzyme shared with saliva.
notes.E: The pancreas secretes trypsinogen, which is activated in the small intestine. Salivary glands do not supply digestive trypsinogen.

questions.stem: The humoral and pharmacological factors inhibiting salivary secretion are:
questions.why: Sympathetic activity (catecholamines, adrenergic agonists) inhibits salivation (causing dry mouth), as do anticholinergics.

notes.A: True, but incomplete.
notes.B: True, but incomplete.
notes.C: True, but incomplete.
notes.E: These STIMULATE saliva.

questions.stem: Saliva:

options.label: A
options.text: from different salivary glands has a similar composition

options.label: B
options.text: contains enzymes essential for the digestion of proteins

options.label: C
options.text: has less than half the ionic calcium level of plasma

options.label: D
options.text: has more than twice the iodide level of plasma

questions.why: The salivary glands can concentrate inorganic iodide from plasma through sodium–iodide symporter activity. Salivary iodide can exceed twice the plasma concentration, although the ratio varies with iodine exposure and flow.

notes.A: Parotid saliva is predominantly serous, while sublingual secretion is relatively rich in mucins. Composition also varies with stimulation.
notes.B: Salivary amylase starts starch digestion. The main digestive proteases act in the stomach and small intestine.
notes.C: Salivary ionised calcium varies with the sample and flow conditions. A fixed ratio below half the plasma value is an unreliable general description.
notes.E: Salivary pH depends on flow and bicarbonate. Stimulated saliva is often near neutral or slightly alkaline.

questions.stem: Swallowing is a reflex which:

options.label: A
options.text: has its reflex centres in the cervical segments of the spinal cord

options.label: B
options.text: is initiated by a voluntary act and includes inhibition of respiration

options.label: C
options.text: has its reflex centres in the thoracic segments of the spinal cord

options.label: D
options.text: is not dependent on intrinsic nerve networks in the oesophagus

options.label: E
options.text: is more effective when the person is lying down rather than when standing

questions.why: The oral phase of swallowing begins voluntarily as the tongue moves the bolus posteriorly. The medullary swallowing pattern then coordinates pharyngeal propulsion, airway closure and a brief pause in breathing.

notes.A: The central swallowing pattern is coordinated in the brainstem, with key control circuits in the medulla.
notes.C: The thoracic spinal cord is not the swallowing centre. Vagal and enteric circuits coordinate oesophageal passage after the pharyngeal phase.
notes.D: The distal smooth-muscle oesophagus has intrinsic neural circuits that help coordinate its peristaltic contractions.
notes.E: Oesophageal peristalsis moves a bolus in either position. When upright, gravity can assist rather than impede passage.

questions.stem: Secretion of saliva increases when:

options.label: B
options.text: the mouth is flushed with fluids with a pH of about 7

options.label: C
options.text: the subject thinks of unappetizing food

options.label: E
options.text: the saliva glands parasympathetic nerve supply is stimulated

questions.why: Parasympathetic stimulation is the primary driver of salivary secretion.

notes.A: Atropine BLOCKS saliva.
notes.B: Neutral fluid is a weak stimulus.
notes.C: Unappetising thoughts inhibit.
notes.D: Adrenaline reduces watery saliva.

questions.stem: Muscle tone in the lower oesophagus is:

options.label: A
options.text: lower than tone in the middle oesophagus

options.label: B
options.text: a major factor in preventing heartburn

questions.why: Resting lower oesophageal sphincter pressure adds to the antireflux barrier at the gastro-oesophageal junction. The sphincter relaxes during swallowing and usually regains tone after the bolus passes.

notes.A: The lower oesophageal sphincter has a sustained resting pressure above that of the adjacent oesophageal body.
notes.C: The antireflux barrier can weaken in pregnancy, with reduced resting pressure or a diminished sphincter response.
notes.D: Pharmacological gastrin can raise sphincter pressure. The normal response varies, so a simple fall in tone is not expected.
notes.E: Cholinergic input supports sphincter contraction. Antimuscarinic drugs can reduce basal pressure rather than reinforce the barrier.

questions.stem: Normal swallowing is dependent on the integrity of the:
questions.why: Swallowing relies heavily on the glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) cranial nerves.

notes.B: Not essential.
notes.C: Chewing.
notes.D: Not involved.
notes.E: Not essential.

questions.stem: Saliva is responsible for all except:

options.label: E
options.text: maintaining the oral pH at about 7.0

questions.why: Saliva starts starch digestion, lubricates the bolus and helps protect the mouth. Complete digestion of protein requires proteases and peptidases acting in the stomach and small intestine.

notes.A: Water and mucins lubricate food and help form a cohesive bolus that can be swallowed.
notes.B: Saliva buffers plaque acids and supplies calcium and phosphate for enamel remineralisation. Both actions help protect against dental caries.
notes.D: Salivary gland cells can concentrate iodide from plasma. Iodide in saliva can contribute to local antimicrobial chemistry.
notes.E: Bicarbonate and other salivary buffers limit oral pH swings, although the pH is not fixed at exactly seven.

questions.stem: Which of the following has the lowest pH?
questions.why: Gastric parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid, so gastric juice has the lowest pH among these secretions. Duodenal bicarbonate then helps neutralise the acidic chyme.

notes.B: Hepatic bile is relatively alkaline and contains bile salts that assist in processing dietary lipids.
notes.C: Pancreatic duct cells secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid, which raises the pH of acidic duodenal contents.
notes.D: Saliva typically has a near-neutral pH, with higher bicarbonate concentrations at higher flow.
notes.E: Intestinal secretions are generally near neutral to alkaline. Duodenal mucus and bicarbonate help protect the surface from gastric acid.

questions.stem: When parietal cells are stimulated, they secrete:
questions.why: Parietal cells release hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor into the gastric lumen. During acid secretion, bicarbonate enters the blood through the basolateral chloride–bicarbonate exchanger, contributing to the postprandial alkaline tide.

notes.B: Hydrochloric acid comes from parietal cells. Pepsinogen is released into gastric glands by chief cells.
notes.C: Hydrogen ions are released into the gastric lumen. Bicarbonate moves to the blood, so it is not part of the parietal cell's luminal output.
notes.D: Intrinsic factor is released into the lumen. Bicarbonate exits at the basolateral side, while hydrochloric acid is the other key luminal product.
notes.E: Mucous epithelial cells secrete mucus, and chief cells release pepsinogen. Neither is the characteristic luminal secretion of parietal cells.

questions.stem: Secretion of HCl by the gastric parietal cells is needed for:
questions.why: Gastric acid produces a low pH that initiates cleavage of inactive pepsinogen to active pepsin. Pepsin then activates further pepsinogen and cleaves dietary proteins in the acidic gastric lumen.

notes.A: Pancreatic lipase acts in the less acidic environment of the small intestine, where bicarbonate neutralises gastric acid.
notes.B: Lingual lipase is secreted as an enzyme that can work in acidic gastric contents. Pepsinogen, by comparison, requires cleavage of an inactive precursor.
notes.C: Intrinsic factor is a binding protein for vitamin B12. Gastric acid helps release dietary B12 from food proteins, rather than activating intrinsic factor.
notes.E: Bile salts form mixed micelles with lipid digestion products in the small intestine. Gastric acid is not the mechanism for this step.

questions.stem: Gastric acid secretion is decreased by:
questions.why: Vagal input normally promotes acid secretion through direct cholinergic effects and indirect stimulation of gastrin and histamine pathways. Inhibiting this input decreases its stimulatory effect on parietal cells.

notes.B: Peptides and amino acids stimulate gastrin release, which can increase acid secretion during the gastric phase.
notes.C: Histamine activates parietal H2 receptors, increasing cAMP and stimulating the gastric proton pump.
notes.D: Acetylcholine stimulates muscarinic receptors on parietal cells and increases acid secretion.
notes.E: Gastric distension activates local and vagovagal reflexes that promote acid secretion during a meal.

questions.stem: This keeps the chyme in the stomach until it reaches the right consistency to pass into the small intestine:
questions.why: The pyloric sphincter controls gastric emptying. Antral contractions drive larger particles back for further grinding when the outlet narrows, while small volumes of suitably processed chyme pass into the duodenum.

notes.A: The oesophageal sphincters regulate entry into the oesophagus or stomach. They do not meter gastric emptying into the intestine.
notes.B: An intrinsic sphincter is a general description and does not specify the muscular ring at the gastric outlet.
notes.C: The cardiac sphincter is the lower oesophageal sphincter at the entrance to the stomach. It helps prevent reflux.
notes.E: The sphincter between the stomach and proximal duodenum is anatomically the pyloric sphincter.

questions.stem: Parietal cells secrete:
questions.why: Parietal cells use an apical hydrogen–potassium ATPase to secrete hydrogen ions into the gastric lumen. Chloride enters the lumen separately, yielding hydrochloric acid. These cells also secrete intrinsic factor.

notes.A: Serotonin is characteristic of enterochromaffin cells. Gastric enterochromaffin-like cells instead release histamine near parietal cells.
notes.B: Surface and neck mucous cells provide gastric mucus. Surface mucus and bicarbonate protect the lining from acid.
notes.C: Pepsinogen is released chiefly by gastric chief cells and becomes active after exposure to gastric acid.
notes.E: G cells, chiefly in the antrum, secrete gastrin and thereby stimulate acid production downstream.

questions.stem: The cells at the base of fundic or oxyntic glands are:
questions.why: Chief cells (peptic cells) are located deep in the gastric glands and secrete pepsinogen.

notes.B: In the antrum.
notes.C: Scattered.
notes.D: Intestinal.
notes.E: Mid-gland, not the base.

questions.stem: Which enzymes are secreted with the gastric juice:

options.label: E
options.text: proteolytic, nucleolytic, lipolytic and amylolytic enzymes

questions.why: Gastric chief cells release pepsinogen and gastric lipase. Acid converts the inactive precursor pepsinogen to pepsin. Hydrochloric acid is also a component of gastric juice, but it is not an enzyme.

notes.B: Trypsinogen is from the pancreas, while maltase activity is located at the small-intestinal brush border.
notes.C: Hydrochloric acid creates the low gastric pH and helps activate pepsinogen. It is an acid rather than a digestive enzyme.
notes.D: Pepsin and gastric lipase handle protein and some fat. Amylase in swallowed material comes mainly from saliva at this point.
notes.E: The pancreas supplies the major digestive nucleases, and digestive amylase comes from the salivary glands and pancreas.

questions.stem: The humoral factors inhibiting gastric motility are:

options.label: B
options.text: GIP, catecholamines, secretin, somatostatin, cholecystokinin- pancreozimin

options.label: E
options.text: intestinal hormones, somatostatin, secretin and cholecystokinin- pancreozimin

questions.why: Enterogastrones (like secretin, CCK, GIP) and catecholamines inhibit gastric motility to slow emptying when the duodenum is busy.

notes.A: Gastrin stimulates motility.
notes.C: Incomplete.
notes.D: Stimulants.
notes.E: Less complete than B.

questions.stem: The humoral factors stimulating gastric motility are:

options.label: A
options.text: catecholamines, secretin, gastric peptide, somatostatin, cholecystokinin- pancreozimin

options.label: D
options.text: GIP, VIP, somatostatin, secretin and cholecystokinin- pancreozimin

questions.why: Motilin promotes strong gastric and upper intestinal contractions during fasting, particularly phase III of the migrating motor complex. Gastrin can stimulate antral motility after a meal.

notes.A: This group includes secretin and cholecystokinin, which can slow gastric emptying during duodenal feedback.
notes.B: Secretin and cholecystokinin help slow delivery from the stomach as the duodenum processes acid and nutrients.
notes.D: This group includes inhibitory gut signals. For example, cholecystokinin slows gastric emptying in response to duodenal fatty acids.
notes.E: Histamine mainly stimulates gastric acid secretion via H2 receptors, and secretin is associated with inhibitory feedback on gastric emptying.

questions.stem: The humoral factors that inhibit gastric secretion are:

options.label: A
options.text: gastrin, histamine, acetylcholine, cholecystokinin-pancreozymin, bombesin, motilin

questions.why: Enterogastrones (GIP, secretin, CCK, VIP) act as hormones to inhibit gastric acid and pepsinogen secretion.

notes.A: Stimulants.
notes.B: Stimulants.
notes.D: Not the main ones.
notes.E: Unrelated.

questions.stem: Which humoral factors stimulate gastric secretion:

options.label: B
options.text: secretin, cholecystokinin-pancreozymin, histamine, acetylcholine, bombesin, motilin

questions.why: Gastrin, histamine and acetylcholine are the three standard stimulators of gastric acid secretion. Gastrin acts largely through histamine release from enterochromaffin-like cells. Histamine is mostly paracrine here, and acetylcholine is a neural transmitter.

notes.A: Somatostatin inhibits acid secretion. Secretin and cholecystokinin participate in intestinal feedback rather than forming the primary acid-stimulatory trio.
notes.B: Histamine and acetylcholine stimulate acid secretion. The list also contains signals such as secretin that have different principal actions.
notes.C: Somatostatin is an inhibitory signal for gastrin and acid secretion, and GIP is not part of the direct acid-stimulatory trio.
notes.D: These mediators are not the standard combination of gastric acid signals that converge on the parietal cell.

questions.stem: The physiological effect of gastrin on gastric secretion is:

options.label: A
options.text: increased amount of gastric juice of high acidity and low proteolytic activity

options.label: B
options.text: increased amount of gastric juice of low acidity and high proteolytic activity

options.label: C
options.text: to decrease the amount of gastric juice

options.label: D
options.text: decreased amount of gastric juice of high acidity and low proteolytic activity

options.label: E
options.text: decreased amount of gastric juice of low acidity

questions.why: Gastrin stimulates parietal cells (acid) more than chief cells (pepsinogen), resulting in high acidity but relatively low proteolytic activity.

notes.B: Reversed.
notes.C: Gastrin INCREASES secretion.
notes.D: Increased, not decreased.
notes.E: Increased, not decreased.

questions.stem: The physiological effect of histamine on gastric secretion is:

options.label: A
options.text: increased amount of gastric juice of high acidity and low proteolytic activity

options.label: B
options.text: to decrease the amount of the gastric juice

options.label: C
options.text: increased amount of gastric juice of low acidity and high proteolytic activity

options.label: D
options.text: increased amount of gastric juice of low acidity and low proteolytic activity

options.label: E
options.text: no change in the amount or acidity of gastric juice

questions.why: Histamine strongly stimulates acid secretion (via H2 receptors) but has little effect on pepsinogen.

notes.B: Histamine INCREASES it.
notes.C: Reversed.
notes.D: Acidity is HIGH.
notes.E: A marked change occurs.

questions.stem: The chief cells of the stomach glands secrete:
questions.why: Gastric chief cells secrete pepsinogen, the precursor to the protease pepsin, as well as gastric lipase. Low gastric pH activates pepsinogen so that protein digestion can begin in the stomach.

notes.B: Hydrochloric acid is secreted by parietal cells via their apical hydrogen–potassium ATPase.
notes.C: Mucous cells at the surface and in the gland neck secrete mucus. Chief cells are distinguished by digestive precursors.
notes.D: Gastrointestinal hormones come from specialised enteroendocrine cells. For example, antral G cells secrete gastrin.
notes.E: Locally acting mediators such as gastric histamine have separate sources. Histamine is released by enterochromaffin-like cells.

questions.stem: In the stomach:

options.label: B
options.text: pepsinogen is converted to pepsin by hydrochloric acid

options.label: C
options.text: ferrous iron is reduced to ferric iron by hydrochloric acid

options.label: D
options.text: acid secretion is inhibited by pentagastrin

options.label: E
options.text: there is a rise in the bacterial count after histamine H1 receptor blockade

questions.why: Hydrochloric acid lowers gastric pH and initiates the activation of pepsinogen to pepsin. Active pepsin then promotes further precursor cleavage and digests proteins under acidic conditions.

notes.A: The fasting stomach commonly has a pH below four. Food can buffer the acid and temporarily raise the pH after a meal.
notes.C: Ferrous iron is already the reduced form. Conversion to ferric iron is oxidation, and gastric acidity helps keep dietary iron soluble.
notes.D: Pentagastrin is a gastrin analogue that stimulates parietal acid output, partly by promoting histamine release.
notes.E: Parietal acid secretion is stimulated through H2 receptors. The expected acid-dependent effect on bacterial survival is not specific to H1 blockade.

questions.stem: The gastric juice:

options.label: A
options.text: is secreted when the vagus nerves are stimulated

options.label: B
options.text: is secreted in vagotomized animals when food is chewed but not swallowed

options.label: C
options.text: activates the digestive enzymes secreted with saliva

options.label: D
options.text: digests the gastric mucosa because it is not protected by a pepsin inactivator

options.label: E
options.text: does not irritate the oesophageal mucosa if regurgitated from the stomach

questions.why: Vagal stimulation evokes gastric juice secretion during the cephalic phase. Cholinergic pathways stimulate secretory cells and vagal–enteric pathways enhance gastrin and histamine signalling to parietal cells.

notes.B: Chewing without swallowing chiefly evokes a vagally mediated cephalic response. Vagotomy markedly decreases this gastric secretory response.
notes.C: Gastric acidity inhibits most salivary amylase activity. Lingual lipase can work in acid, but gastric juice does not generally activate salivary enzymes.
notes.D: The gastric mucosa has a protective mucus–bicarbonate barrier, a tight epithelium and mucosal blood flow that limit injury from acid and pepsin.
notes.E: Refluxed gastric juice can irritate or injure oesophageal mucosa, where protection from prolonged acid exposure is weaker.

questions.stem: The normally innervated stomach:

options.label: A
options.text: is stimulated to secrete gastric juice when food is chewed, even if it is not swallowed

options.label: B
options.text: secrete HCl when its H1- histamine receptors are blocked

options.label: C
options.text: increases gastric secretion when there are fear and depression

options.label: D
options.text: empties slower than the denervated stomach

options.label: E
options.text: is stimulated to secrete gastric juice by the hormone secretin

questions.why: Chewing and tasting food activate the cephalic phase before food reaches the stomach. Intact vagal pathways mediate the gastric secretory response to this form of sham feeding.

notes.B: The relevant histamine receptor for stimulation of acid secretion is H2 on parietal cells. Blocking H1 is not a stimulus.
notes.C: The effect of emotional states on gastric secretion can vary. Chewing and tasting are reproducible cephalic-phase stimuli.
notes.D: Gastric emptying depends on accommodation, antral contractions and pyloric coordination. The relative speed after denervation varies with the meal and conditions.
notes.E: Secretin is released in response to duodenal acid and mainly stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate. It does not drive gastric acid secretion.

questions.stem: Secretion of gastric juice:

options.label: A
options.text: decreases when food stimulates mucosal cells in the pyloric region

options.label: B
options.text: is associated with a decrease in the pH of venous blood draining the stomach

options.label: C
options.text: in response to food is increased after vagotomy

options.label: E
options.text: is essential for absorption of vitamin B12

questions.why: Intrinsic factor in gastric juice binds vitamin B12 after it is transferred from haptocorrin in the small intestine. The intrinsic factor–B12 complex is then taken up by receptors in the terminal ileum.

notes.A: Food peptides in the pyloric antrum stimulate G-cell gastrin release, which increases gastric acid secretion.
notes.B: Acid secretion adds bicarbonate to the gastric venous blood. This produces a transient rise in pH called the alkaline tide.
notes.C: Vagal innervation supports the cephalic and gastric secretory responses. Vagotomy decreases the neural contribution to secretion.
notes.D: Salivary and pancreatic amylase plus intestinal brush-border enzymes provide the main steps for carbohydrate digestion.

questions.stem: Peptic ulcer pain is typically relieved by:

options.label: A
options.text: raising the pH of the fluid bathing the ulcer and a drug blocking the gastric proton pump

options.label: D
options.text: a drug which interferes with the action of acetylcholinesterase

options.label: E
options.text: a drug which stimulates the gastric proton pump

questions.why: A proton-pump inhibitor suppresses acid secretion by blocking the gastric hydrogen–potassium ATPase. The subsequent rise in intragastric pH lowers acid exposure at the ulcer and can relieve pain as healing proceeds.

notes.B: Lowering the pH increases acidity and can increase acid exposure at the injured surface.
notes.C: Stimulating H2 receptors increases parietal acid secretion. H2 receptor antagonists can instead suppress acid output.
notes.D: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor increases the availability of acetylcholine and does not provide standard acid suppression for ulcers.
notes.E: The gastric proton pump increases delivery of hydrogen ions to the lumen. Stimulating it would increase acid exposure.

questions.stem: Gastric:

options.label: A
options.text: acid secretion in response to a lowered blood sugar is mediated by the hormone gastrin

options.label: B
options.text: emptying is facilitated by sympathetic nerve activity

options.label: C
options.text: acid secretion increases when histamine H2, muscarinic M1 or gastrin receptors are activated

options.label: D
options.text: acid secretion is inhibited by the presence of food in the duodenum

questions.why: Gastric acid secretion is stimulated by histamine (H2), ACh (M3/M1), and gastrin. It is inhibited by enterogastrones when food (especially fat/acid) enters the duodenum.

notes.A: Vagal, not gastrin.
notes.B: Sympathetic SLOWS emptying.
notes.C: True, but so is D.
notes.D: True, but so is C.

questions.stem: Which of the following are incorrectly paired:
questions.why: Renin is a kidney protease that cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I. Milk coagulation is associated with chymosin, historically called rennin, which cleaves a casein component. The two enzymes have different substrates.

notes.A: Pancreatic alpha-amylase hydrolyses internal alpha-1,4 bonds in starch, producing smaller carbohydrates.
notes.B: Pancreatic elastase can digest elastin and other proteins. It is secreted as a precursor activated in the intestinal lumen.
notes.D: Enteropeptidase at the duodenal brush border activates trypsinogen by cutting its activation peptide.
notes.E: Phospholipase A2 releases the fatty acid at the second position of a phospholipid backbone by hydrolysing its ester bond.

questions.stem: Secretion of the intrinsic factor of Castle occurs in:
questions.why: Gastric parietal cells in the oxyntic glands secrete intrinsic factor as well as hydrochloric acid. Intrinsic factor is needed for normal receptor-mediated vitamin B12 uptake in the terminal ileum.

notes.B: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and gastric lipase. Intrinsic factor comes from the neighbouring parietal cells.
notes.C: The upper abdomen is an anatomical region. The specific source is the parietal cell in the gastric body and fundus.
notes.D: The alpha cells of pancreatic islets release glucagon into the circulation, not a luminal protein needed for B12 uptake.
notes.E: Parotid acini provide watery saliva containing amylase. Salivary B12-binding haptocorrin is distinct from gastric intrinsic factor.

questions.stem: Gastrin secretion is increased by:

options.label: A
options.text: acid in the lumen of stomach

questions.why: Vagal activation stimulates antral G cells through enteric neurons that release gastrin-releasing peptide. The resulting gastrin raises acid output, largely by promoting release of histamine from enterochromaffin-like cells.

notes.A: Low antral pH stimulates D-cell somatostatin output, which inhibits gastrin release by negative feedback.
notes.B: Calcitonin is primarily involved in calcium regulation. It is not the usual stimulus for meal-related gastrin secretion.
notes.C: Secretin is released in response to acid in the duodenum and promotes bicarbonate secretion. It does not mediate the vagal gastrin response.
notes.E: Luminal gastric acid inhibits gastrin release, and calcitonin does not account for the normal vagal stimulus.

questions.stem: The gastrin is secreted in the:
questions.why: Gastrin is primarily secreted by G cells located in the gastric antrum.

notes.B: Parietal and chief cells.
notes.C: Minor.
notes.D: None.
notes.E: None.

questions.stem: The motor activity of the stomach includes:
questions.why: The stomach accommodates meals by receptive relaxation and uses antral peristalsis both to mix and propel its contents. It also shows periodic contractions during fasting as part of the migrating motor complex.

notes.A: During fasting, the migrating motor complex includes intermittent strong contractions that help clear residual contents.
notes.B: Propulsive contractions move gastric contents toward the pylorus. A portion of liquid and fine particles can enter the duodenum.
notes.C: Antral contractions can mix gastric contents when the pyloric outlet narrows and chyme moves back into the stomach.
notes.D: Receptive relaxation of the proximal stomach accommodates a swallowed meal with little early rise in intragastric pressure.

questions.stem: In the stomach:

options.label: B
options.text: pepsinogen is converted into pepsin under the influence of HCl

options.label: C
options.text: Fe2+ is oxidised to Fe3+ under the influence of HCl

options.label: D
options.text: HCl secretion is suppressed by pentagastrin

options.label: E
options.text: the bacterial count increases after applying H1-receptor blockers

questions.why: Acid secreted by parietal cells lowers gastric pH and initiates conversion of pepsinogen to active pepsin. Active pepsin then helps activate additional pepsinogen and hydrolyses dietary protein.

notes.A: Gastric pH is often well below four when fasting, although food can buffer the lumen temporarily.
notes.C: Gastric acidity helps keep non-haem iron soluble. The ferrous form is the reduced form used for uptake by the intestinal divalent metal transporter.
notes.D: Pentagastrin stimulates gastric acid output because it acts as an analogue of the hormone gastrin.
notes.E: Histamine stimulates parietal acid secretion through H2 receptors. Blocking H1 is not the usual mechanism for loss of the gastric acid barrier.

questions.stem: The lowest pH is characteristic of the:
questions.why: Gastric juice has the lowest pH of these digestive fluids because parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid. Saliva and the fluids entering the duodenum are buffered and are usually much less acidic.

notes.B: Bile contains bile salts and bicarbonate and is generally mildly alkaline before mixing with gastric contents.
notes.C: Pancreatic juice is bicarbonate rich and raises the pH of duodenal contents after gastric emptying.
notes.D: Saliva contains bicarbonate buffers, whose concentrations vary with flow. Its pH is generally far above that of gastric juice.
notes.E: Small-intestinal fluid and duodenal mucus are generally nearer neutral and help protect the mucosa from gastric acid.

questions.stem: Release of which one of the following increases the pH of duodenal contents?
questions.why: Acidic chyme stimulates duodenal S cells to release secretin. Secretin stimulates pancreatic duct cells to secrete bicarbonate, which buffers incoming hydrogen ions and raises the pH in the duodenal lumen.

notes.B: Gastrin increases gastric acid output. It does not supply the feedback signal for pancreatic bicarbonate secretion.
notes.C: Intrinsic factor binds vitamin B12 for ileal uptake and has no major role in duodenal buffering.
notes.D: Cholecystokinin stimulates pancreatic enzyme release and gallbladder contraction. Secretin is the principal signal for bicarbonate output when acid arrives.
notes.E: Gastrin-releasing peptide stimulates antral G cells, which can increase gastric acid production during vagal activation.

questions.stem: In the duodenum in response to acidic chyme is released:
questions.why: Duodenal S cells release secretin in response to acid delivered from the stomach. The hormone increases bicarbonate-rich pancreatic and biliary secretion to buffer the duodenal contents.

notes.A: Cholecystokinin is released mainly in response to fatty acids and peptide products and stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion.
notes.B: Gastrin is secreted chiefly by antral G cells. Peptides and vagal stimulation increase gastrin, while low antral pH restrains it.
notes.D: Many intestinal hormones are peptides. The specific peptide released from S cells in response to acid is secretin.
notes.E: Amylase is a digestive enzyme released by pancreatic acini and salivary glands. It does not signal the response to low duodenal pH.

questions.stem: Which enzymes are secreted with the pancreatic juice:

options.label: B
options.text: proteolytic: trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, elastase, carboxypeptidase, etc.

questions.why: Pancreatic juice contains hydrolases for lipids, proteins, starch and nucleic acids. Many pancreatic proteases leave acinar cells as inactive precursors. Enteropeptidase initiates their activation in the intestine by generating trypsin.

notes.A: Pancreatic lipase releases fatty acids from triglycerides, and pancreatic carboxyl ester lipase acts on other lipid esters.
notes.B: Trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, proelastase and procarboxypeptidases are secreted precursors of pancreatic proteases.
notes.C: Pancreatic alpha-amylase hydrolyses internal alpha-1,4 bonds in starch to yield smaller carbohydrates.
notes.D: Pancreatic ribonucleases and deoxyribonucleases are secreted into the gut lumen to hydrolyse dietary RNA and DNA.

questions.stem: Which of the bile components are important for digestion:
questions.why: Bile salts and phospholipids form mixed aggregates that help disperse dietary lipids and carry digested lipids in the aqueous lumen. Cholesterol is another major biliary lipid carried in these aggregates. The detergent action comes chiefly from the bile salts.

notes.A: Secretin increases bicarbonate-rich biliary and pancreatic secretion. The listed regulators are not digestive constituents of bile.
notes.C: Acid phosphatase does not provide the physiologically important detergent action. Secretin regulates ductal secretion from the circulation.
notes.D: Pancreatic juice supplies major proteases, lipases and amylase. Bile supports digestion through bile salts and other lipids.
notes.E: Cholecystokinin stimulates gallbladder contraction and enzyme secretion by pancreatic acini. It is a hormone rather than a biliary digestive lipid.

questions.stem: The humoral factors that stimulate the formation and secretion of bile are:

options.label: C
options.text: secretin, gastrin, cholecystokinin- pancreozimin, bile salts

questions.why: Secretin stimulates bile duct secretion (bicarbonate), while CCK stimulates gallbladder contraction. Bile salts stimulate their own secretion via enterohepatic circulation.

notes.A: Not choleretic.
notes.B: Not choleretic.
notes.D: Catecholamines inhibit.
notes.E: Enzymes.

questions.stem: The humoral factors that inhibit the formation and secretion of bile are:

options.label: E
options.text: insulin, glucagon, catecholamines, growth hormone, glucocorticoids, thyroid hormones

questions.why: Sympathetic stimulation (catecholamines) generally inhibits bile secretion and gallbladder contraction.

notes.A: Stimulants.
notes.C: Enzymes.
notes.D: Not inhibitors.
notes.E: Mixed list.

questions.stem: The humoral factors that stimulate the secretion of pancreatic juice are:

options.label: C
options.text: secretin, cholecystokinin- pancreozimin, gastrin, serotonin, VIP, insulin

options.label: E
options.text: glucagon, insulin, catecholamines, growth hormone, glucocorticoids, thyroid hormones

questions.why: Secretin (bicarbonate) and CCK (enzymes) are the primary stimulants of pancreatic exocrine secretion.

notes.A: Somatostatin INHIBITS.
notes.B: Enzymes, not stimuli.
notes.D: Somatostatin inhibits.
notes.E: Mixed list.

questions.stem: As far as bile is considered:

options.label: A
options.text: contains enzymes required for the digestion of fat

options.label: C
options.text: bile salts make cholesterol more water- soluble

options.label: E
options.text: becomes more alkaline during storage in the gallbladder

questions.why: Bile salts act as detergents to emulsify fats and cholesterol, making them soluble in the aqueous chyme.

notes.A: Bile has NO enzymes.
notes.B: Bilirubin is CONJUGATED.
notes.D: Iron is removed.
notes.E: It becomes more ACIDIC.

questions.stem: Pancreatic secretion:

options.label: A
options.text: in response to vagal stimulation is copious, rich in bicarbonate but poor in enzymes

options.label: B
options.text: in response to acid in the duodenum is scanty but rich in enzymes

options.label: C
options.text: in response to secretin secretion is low in bicarbonate

options.label: D
options.text: contains enzymes that digest neutral fat to glycerol and fatty acids

options.label: E
options.text: contains enzymes that convert disaccharides to monosaccharides

questions.why: Pancreatic juice contains enzymes for neutral-fat digestion. Pancreatic triglyceride lipase chiefly releases two fatty acids and a 2-monoacylglycerol. Further hydrolysis by intestinal and pancreatic esterases can yield free glycerol.

notes.A: Vagal cholinergic input promotes secretion from pancreatic acini. The characteristic copious bicarbonate-rich response is driven mainly by secretin.
notes.B: Duodenal acid stimulates secretin release, producing an abundant watery secretion rich in bicarbonate.
notes.C: Secretin primarily acts on pancreatic ducts, where it increases bicarbonate and fluid secretion.
notes.E: Disaccharides are converted to monosaccharides mainly by enzymes in the small-intestinal brush border. Pancreatic amylase acts on larger carbohydrates.

questions.stem: The liver is the principal site for:
questions.why: The liver synthesizes most plasma proteins, most notably albumin.

notes.B: Immunoglobulins come from plasma cells.
notes.C: Only bacteria make B12.
notes.D: Vitamin C is not stored mainly there.
notes.E: Not its principal role.

questions.stem: The passage of acidic gastric contents to the duodenum may cause:

options.label: A
options.text: copious secretion of pancreatic juice rich in bicarbonate

options.label: D
options.text: contraction of the sphincter of Oddi

questions.why: Acid delivered to the duodenum stimulates S cells to release secretin. Pancreatic ducts respond with a large volume of bicarbonate-rich fluid, which buffers the acidic chyme.

notes.B: The duodenal response to acid can slow gastric emptying so that acid enters at a rate the intestine can buffer.
notes.C: Gallbladder contraction is promoted by cholecystokinin, particularly when fat reaches the duodenum. Acid primarily evokes the secretin response here.
notes.D: During meal-related bile delivery, the sphincter of Oddi generally relaxes with cholecystokinin signalling. The acid-triggered secretin response is pancreatic buffering.
notes.E: Pancreozymin is the older name for cholecystokinin. Duodenal acid selectively stimulates secretin in this comparison.

questions.stem: Bile salts:

options.label: A
options.text: derived from cholesterol, are the only constituents of bile necessary for digestion

options.label: B
options.text: have a characteristic molecule, being water-soluble

options.label: C
options.text: are reabsorbed mainly in the upper small intestine

questions.why: Bile salts are synthesized from cholesterol and are the essential component of bile for fat emulsification and digestion.

notes.B: They are amphipathic.
notes.C: TERMINAL ileum.
notes.D: They DECREASE surface tension.
notes.E: Ileum.

questions.stem: The cells of the liver:

options.label: A
options.text: help to maintain the normal blood glucose level

options.label: B
options.text: deaminate amino acids to form NH4+ which is excreted as ammonium salts in the urine

options.label: D
options.text: manufacture most of the immune globulins

options.label: E
options.text: activate steroid hormones manufactured in the gonads

questions.why: The liver buffers blood glucose across feeding and fasting. Hepatocytes store glucose as glycogen after a meal and maintain circulating glucose between meals by glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

notes.B: Hepatic amino acid catabolism produces nitrogen that is converted mainly to urea. Renal glutamine metabolism is a major source of ammonia excreted as ammonium.
notes.C: UV light supports cholecalciferol synthesis in the skin. The liver hydroxylates cholecalciferol to 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
notes.D: Immunoglobulins are produced by plasma cells. The liver synthesises albumin and many other non-antibody plasma proteins.
notes.E: Gonadal steroid hormones act on receptors in target tissues. The liver is important for steroid metabolism and clearance.

questions.stem: Urobilinogen is:

options.label: A
options.text: a mixture of colourless compounds also known as stercobilinogen

options.label: B
options.text: formed in the reticuloendothelial system from bilirubin

questions.why: Urobilinogen is formed by bacterial action in the gut. Some is excreted in feces, and some is reabsorbed into the blood and excreted in urine.

notes.A: True, but so is C.
notes.B: Formed by gut bacteria.
notes.C: True, but so is A.
notes.D: Mainly faeces.

questions.stem: Lack of pancreatic juice in the duodenum may lead to:

options.label: A
options.text: the presence of undigested meat fibres in the stools

options.label: B
options.text: an increase in the fat content of the faeces

options.label: C
options.text: a decrease in the fat of the faeces

options.label: D
options.text: a high prothrombin level in blood

questions.why: Pancreatic juice supplies protease precursors and lipase. A marked lack of pancreatic enzymes can leave undigested muscle fibres in the stool and increases faecal fat by impairing triglyceride digestion.

notes.A: Reduced pancreatic protease delivery can leave muscle fibres incompletely digested. Their increased presence in stool is called creatorrhoea.
notes.B: Reduced pancreatic lipase delivery can impair triglyceride digestion and increase faecal fat. This is steatorrhoea.
notes.C: Fat maldigestion increases the loss of fat into faeces rather than decreasing it.
notes.D: Severe fat malabsorption can reduce vitamin K uptake and impair activation of prothrombin and other vitamin K-dependent clotting proteins.

questions.stem: Which of the following has the highest pH:
questions.why: Pancreatic juice is usually the most alkaline of these fluids because duct cells secrete a high concentration of bicarbonate, especially during secretin stimulation. Actual pH varies with the secretion rate and sampling conditions.

notes.A: Gastric juice is acidic because parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid into the gastric lumen.
notes.C: Gallbladder bile is concentrated and can be acidified during storage, lowering its pH relative to freshly secreted hepatic bile.
notes.D: Intestinal secretions can be alkaline, but pancreatic ducts provide the especially bicarbonate-rich secretion that neutralises most incoming acid.
notes.E: Saliva contains bicarbonate and varies with flow. It is commonly near neutral or mildly alkaline.

questions.stem: Secretin is released by:
questions.why: Secretin is released by enteroendocrine S cells in the proximal small intestine when gastric acid reaches the duodenum. It increases pancreatic and biliary bicarbonate secretion to neutralise the acid.

notes.B: Acid in the stomach does not directly contact duodenal S cells. The stimulus occurs when acidic chyme crosses the pylorus.
notes.C: Bile ducts respond to secretin by increasing bicarbonate output. The liver is not the primary site of secretin production.
notes.D: Colonic distension activates local and reflex motility pathways. Duodenal acid is the classic stimulus for secretin.
notes.E: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile and contracts in response to cholecystokinin. Secretin comes from proximal intestinal S cells.

questions.stem: Choleretica are substances, which:

options.label: B
options.text: stimulate the secretion of bile by the liver

options.label: D
options.text: suppress the secretion of bile by the liver

questions.why: Choleretic agents increase bile secretion by the liver or biliary duct system. This is distinct from expelling bile already stored in the gallbladder, an effect termed cholagogue or cholekinetic.

notes.A: Gallbladder contraction increases delivery of stored bile. This is a cholekinetic effect, as seen with cholecystokinin.
notes.C: Pancreatic secretion concerns fluid and enzymes from pancreatic ducts and acini. Choleresis refers to biliary output.
notes.D: Suppression of hepatic bile secretion is the opposite of a choleretic effect.
notes.E: Inhibiting gallbladder emptying delays delivery from storage. It does not define an effect on hepatic bile formation.

questions.stem: Enterohepatic circle refers to:
questions.why: Enterohepatic circulation classically describes bile salts cycling from liver to intestine and back. Most are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum, return to the liver via portal blood and are secreted again in bile.

notes.A: Dietary proteins are digested to amino acids and small peptides. Their absorption is not the classic liver–bile–ileum cycle.
notes.B: Most long-chain dietary fats are carried from the intestine in lymph within chylomicrons. Bile salts assist absorption and then cycle separately.
notes.C: Monosaccharides travel through portal blood to the liver after absorption. They do not enter the classic bile-salt recycling pathway.
notes.E: Some urobilinogen derived from bilirubin also recirculates. The standard high-volume digestive recycling pathway refers to bile salts.

questions.stem: Trypsinogen is converted into trypsin under the influence of:
questions.why: Enteropeptidase, also called enterokinase, is a brush-border protease in the proximal small intestine. It cleaves the activation peptide from trypsinogen. The resulting trypsin activates more trypsinogen and several other pancreatic zymogens.

notes.A: Gastric acid initiates pepsinogen activation in the stomach. Trypsinogen is activated enzymatically in the small intestine.
notes.B: Iron salts play no physiological role in trypsinogen activation. Enteropeptidase supplies the initiating proteolytic cleavage.
notes.D: Gastrin is a hormone that increases gastric acid secretion. It does not cleave a pancreatic zymogen.
notes.E: Acetylcholine stimulates pancreatic secretion through cholinergic pathways. Activation takes place after the zymogen reaches the intestinal lumen.

questions.stem: Which are the bile components of basic significance for digestion:
questions.why: Bile salts are amphipathic molecules that help emulsify fat and form mixed micelles with products of lipid digestion. These micelles deliver fatty acids and monoacylglycerols through the aqueous layer near the intestinal brush border.

notes.A: Secretin regulates bicarbonate-rich secretion into bile and pancreatic juice. Such regulatory hormones are distinct from bile salts in the lumen.
notes.C: Acid phosphatase lacks the detergent action that makes bile salts important for intestinal lipid processing.
notes.D: The pancreas supplies the major luminal digestive enzymes. Bile promotes lipid digestion by dispersing and solubilising lipids.
notes.E: Cholecystokinin stimulates delivery of bile from the gallbladder. The hormone does not itself form luminal mixed micelles.

questions.stem: Calcium absorption is facilitated by:
questions.why: Calcitriol is the active vitamin D metabolite. It increases intestinal calcium absorption, particularly the regulated transcellular pathway, by promoting expression of transport proteins such as TRPV6 and calbindin.

notes.A: Hypercalcaemia lowers parathyroid hormone secretion, which can reduce renal calcitriol production. It is not the usual stimulus for calcium uptake.
notes.B: Oxalate can form poorly soluble complexes with calcium in the intestine and decrease the amount available for absorption.
notes.C: Iron overload is not a physiological signal for intestinal calcium transport. The regulated pathway responds primarily to calcitriol.
notes.E: Sodium-coupled transport is important for glucose and several other nutrients, but calcitriol is the principal regulator of active intestinal calcium uptake.

questions.stem: Fat absorption occurs mainly in the:
questions.why: Fat digestion and absorption primarily begin in the duodenum, where bile and pancreatic lipase are released.

notes.A: Little is absorbed there.
notes.C: Bile salts, not fat, are absorbed there.
notes.D: Fat is gone by the caecum.
notes.E: Fat is gone by the colon.

questions.stem: The movements of the small intestine are:
questions.why: The small intestine has mixing contractions, especially segmentation, and propulsive contractions, especially peristalsis. Segmentation improves contact with digestive fluids and the mucosa, while propulsion moves contents distally.

notes.A: Segmentation is a pattern of local contractions that mixes chyme and exposes it to the epithelial surface.
notes.B: Coordinated peristaltic contractions propel chyme along the small intestine as part of normal transit.
notes.C: Retrograde movement can occur in particular patterns. It is not one of the two standard categories of small-intestinal motility named here.
notes.D: Hunger contractions usually refer to contractions felt in the empty stomach. The fasting small intestine has a migrating motor complex.

questions.stem: Where the protein hydrolysis occurs:
questions.why: Protein hydrolysis begins in the stomach through pepsin. In the small intestine, pancreatic proteases and intestinal peptidases continue the process to amino acids and small absorbable peptides.

notes.A: The mouth begins mechanical breakdown and some starch digestion. It does not provide the main digestive proteases for food protein.
notes.B: Acid activates pepsin and denatures dietary proteins. Pepsin hydrolyses peptide bonds in the stomach.
notes.C: Pancreatic trypsin, chymotrypsin and other proteases act in the small intestine, where brush-border and intracellular peptidases complete digestion.
notes.D: The oesophagus transports the swallowed bolus. It does not make a significant contribution to protein hydrolysis.

questions.stem: After a fatty meal is taken, most of the fat would be:

options.label: A
options.text: absorbed in the portal circulation and transported to the liver

options.label: B
options.text: absorbed in the portal vein and transported in the hepatic artery

options.label: C
options.text: absorbed as chylomicrons in the lymphatic system

options.label: D
options.text: absorbed as triglycerides into the portal vein and bypasses the liver

questions.why: After long-chain lipid digestion, enterocytes re-esterify fatty acids and monoacylglycerols to triglycerides. They package those triglycerides into chylomicrons, which enter villus lacteals and reach the blood through the thoracic duct.

notes.A: Shorter-chain fatty acids can reach the liver by portal blood. Most dietary long-chain triglyceride uses the lymphatic route after processing.
notes.B: The portal vein and hepatic artery are separate hepatic inflows. Chylomicrons leave the intestine in lymph before reaching the systemic circulation.
notes.D: Newly formed long-chain triglyceride is carried in chylomicrons in lymph. Portal transport is important for shorter-chain fatty acids.
notes.E: Absorption takes place in the proximal small intestine, including the jejunum. The principal transport mechanism for most meal fat is chylomicron entry into lymph.

questions.stem: For fat digestion:

options.label: A
options.text: bile salts are the most efficient emulsifiers

options.label: B
options.text: gastric lipase is the most important

options.label: C
options.text: pancreatic lipase in the duodenum is needed

questions.why: Pancreatic lipase is the major enzyme for intestinal triglyceride digestion in adults. With colipase at the oil–water interface, it releases fatty acids and 2-monoacylglycerol. Bile-salt micelles then carry those products toward the brush border.

notes.A: Bile salts and phospholipids help disperse lipid droplets. Emulsification improves access but does not itself hydrolyse triglycerides.
notes.B: Gastric lipase contributes to initial lipolysis. Pancreatic lipase normally supplies the greater share of adult triglyceride digestion.
notes.D: Triglyceride hydrolysis occurs mainly at the surface of emulsion droplets. Mixed micelles carry the resulting lipid products.
notes.E: Lipids leave mixed micelles near the epithelial surface and can then enter enterocytes. Whole micelles do not require a dedicated uptake receptor.

questions.stem: In the small intestine, glucose is absorbed:

options.label: B
options.text: by secondary active transport (coupled to Na+ transport)

questions.why: Apical SGLT1 carries glucose into small-intestinal enterocytes together with sodium. The basolateral sodium–potassium ATPase maintains the sodium gradient that drives this secondary active uptake, and glucose exits toward the blood largely through GLUT2.

notes.A: Luminal glucose uptake commonly takes place against a glucose gradient, so passive diffusion alone cannot explain it.
notes.C: Facilitated diffusion through GLUT2 is important for basolateral exit. The principal apical route is sodium-coupled SGLT1.
notes.D: The driving ion for SGLT1 is sodium. Chloride transport follows separate pathways and is not coupled directly to glucose by this transporter.
notes.E: The standard intestinal uptake pathway uses SGLT1 and GLUT2. It is not dependent on insulin-stimulated GLUT4 insertion.

questions.stem: After ingestion of a meal:

options.label: A
options.text: digestion of fat and carbohydrate begins in the mouth while protein digestion begins in the stomach

options.label: B
options.text: carbohydrates are digested in the stomach and proteins in the mouth

options.label: C
options.text: proteins are digested in the mouth and fats and carbohydrates in the stomach

options.label: D
options.text: most fluid and electrolytes are absorbed in the large bowel

options.label: E
options.text: composition of the food has no effect on transit time through the bowel

questions.why: Salivary amylase starts breaking down starch in the mouth, and lingual lipase is released there, with much of its action occurring later in the stomach. Protein digestion starts substantially in the stomach, where acid activates pepsin.

notes.B: Some starch hydrolysis can continue briefly in the stomach, but digestive protein hydrolysis starts primarily there rather than in the mouth.
notes.C: The important early oral carbohydrate enzyme is salivary amylase. The first substantial protein hydrolysis is by gastric pepsin.
notes.D: Most luminal water and electrolytes are absorbed in the small intestine. The colon salvages much of what remains.
notes.E: Meal composition can affect transit. For example, fat entering the duodenum can release signals that slow gastric emptying.

questions.stem: Calcium uptake in the intestine:

options.label: B
options.text: requires a carrier protein on the mucosal side

options.label: D
options.text: is less than 10% of dietary intake

questions.why: Active calcium absorption requires a calcium-binding carrier protein (calbindin) on the mucosal side of the enterocyte.

notes.A: Mainly active (when intake is low).
notes.C: Not simple facilitated diffusion.
notes.D: About 30% is absorbed.
notes.E: Phosphate binds calcium.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a water soluble vitamin?
questions.why: The B vitamins are water-soluble, as is vitamin C. Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble and use intestinal lipid handling for their usual absorption.

notes.A: Vitamin A is fat-soluble. Dietary retinoids use bile-dependent lipid processing and enter chylomicrons after absorption.
notes.C: Vitamin D is fat-soluble. Its active metabolite calcitriol increases intestinal calcium absorption.
notes.D: Vitamin E is fat-soluble and reaches the circulation in lipoproteins after intestinal absorption.
notes.E: Vitamin K is fat-soluble and is needed for activation of several clotting proteins through gamma-carboxylation.

questions.stem: The function of the ileum is to:

options.label: B
options.text: absorb vitamin B12 and bile salts

questions.why: The terminal ileum is uniquely responsible for the absorption of vitamin B12 (with intrinsic factor) and the reabsorption of bile salts.

notes.A: Mostly jejunum.
notes.C: Duodenum.
notes.D: Stomach.
notes.E: Only B is specific.

questions.stem: The enzymes, secreted with the intestinal juice are:

options.label: A
options.text: exopeptidases, lipase, maltase, nucleic (nuclease, nucleotidases, nucleosidases)

options.label: B
options.text: endo- and exopeptidases, esterase and amylolytic enzymes

options.label: D
options.text: aminopeptidase, dipeptidase, nuclease, somatostatin, secretin, cholecystokinin- pancreozimin

questions.why: Intestinal juice (succus entericus) contains enzymes like aminopeptidase, dipeptidase, nuclease, and lipase for final digestion.

notes.A: Maltase is brush border.
notes.B: Endopeptidases are pancreatic.
notes.D: Hormones are not enzymes.
notes.E: Pancreatic.

questions.stem: The humoral factors that stimulate intestinal motility are:

options.label: C
options.text: cholecystokinin-pancreozymin, motilin, gastrin, substance P and serotonin

questions.why: Several gut hormones including CCK, VIP, and substance P stimulate intestinal motility.

notes.A: Catecholamines inhibit.
notes.B: Secretin inhibits.
notes.D: Too vague.
notes.E: Secretin inhibits.

questions.stem: The carbohydrates are absorbed as:
questions.why: Digestible carbohydrates are absorbed as monosaccharides. The main dietary products are the hexoses glucose, galactose and fructose. Absorbable pentoses are also monosaccharides.

notes.A: Disaccharides normally require digestion by brush-border enzymes before their component monosaccharides can be absorbed.
notes.B: Glycogen is a polysaccharide. Digestion releases smaller products that are converted to glucose before absorption.
notes.D: Glucosamine is an amino sugar, but it is not the general form in which dietary carbohydrates are absorbed.
notes.E: Glucose can be absorbed, whereas glycogen normally requires prior hydrolysis. This is not the usual set of absorptive products.

questions.stem: Defaecation is a reflex action:

options.label: A
options.text: that is coordinated by reflex centres in the sacral cord

options.label: B
options.text: whose afferent limb carries impulses from stretch receptors in the colon

options.label: C
options.text: whose efferent limb travels mainly in sympathetic autonomic nerves

options.label: D
options.text: which is more likely to be initiated just before a meal than just after it

options.label: E
options.text: which can be involuntarily inhibited or facilitated

questions.why: The defecation reflex is coordinated by the sacral segments of the spinal cord (S2-S4).

notes.B: From the RECTUM.
notes.C: Parasympathetic (pelvic).
notes.D: More likely AFTER (gastrocolic reflex).
notes.E: VOLUNTARILY.

questions.stem: Intestinal juice contain:

options.label: A
options.text: potassium in a concentration similar to that in extracellular fluid

options.label: B
options.text: enzymes that are released when the vagus nerve is inhibited

options.label: E
options.text: enzymes that suppress pancreatic proteolytic enzymes

questions.why: Intestinal juice contains disaccharidases (like maltase, sucrase, lactase) to break disaccharides into monosaccharides.

notes.A: Potassium is higher.
notes.B: Vagal stimulation releases them.
notes.D: Monosaccharides are not hydrolysed further.
notes.E: Not true.

questions.stem: In the small intestine:

options.label: A
options.text: the enzyme concentration in intestinal juice is higher in the ileum than in the jejunum

options.label: B
options.text: vitamin B12 is absorbed mainly in the jejunum

options.label: C
options.text: water absorption is independent on the active absorption of sodium and glucose

options.label: D
options.text: absorption of calcium occurs mainly in the terminal ileum

options.label: E
options.text: glucose absorption is dependent on sodium absorption

questions.why: The main apical glucose transporter in intestinal enterocytes, SGLT1, couples glucose uptake to downhill sodium entry. The sodium gradient is maintained by the basolateral sodium–potassium ATPase.

notes.A: The distribution depends on the enzyme. Many enzymes are delivered to the proximal lumen from the pancreas, while many intestinal enzymes remain at the brush border.
notes.B: Intrinsic factor–bound vitamin B12 is taken up mainly in the terminal ileum.
notes.C: Sodium and nutrient absorption create an osmotic gradient that promotes water absorption, as exploited by oral rehydration solutions.
notes.D: Regulated calcium absorption is especially important in the duodenum and proximal small intestine. The terminal ileum is specialised for B12 and bile-salt uptake.

questions.stem: Absorption of dietary fat:

options.label: A
options.text: can only occur after the neutral fat has been split into glycerol and fatty acids

options.label: B
options.text: does not depend on their size

options.label: C
options.text: is impaired when bile salt reabsorption is prevented by resection of the terminal ileum

options.label: D
options.text: is carried out by passive diffusion

options.label: E
options.text: is greatest in the lower parts of the small intestine

questions.why: Extensive terminal ileal resection can prevent enough bile-salt reabsorption to deplete the bile-salt pool. This limits mixed-micelle formation and impairs absorption of the products of long-chain fat digestion.

notes.A: The main products of pancreatic triglyceride digestion are free fatty acids and 2-monoacylglycerol. Complete splitting to glycerol is not required.
notes.B: Fatty acid chain length affects absorption and transport. Shorter-chain fatty acids can enter portal blood more readily than long-chain products.
notes.D: Some lipid products can cross membranes by diffusion, but carrier-assisted uptake, intracellular processing and lymphatic transport also contribute to absorption.
notes.E: Dietary lipid absorption is most important in the proximal small bowel. The terminal ileum mainly recovers bile salts for reuse.

questions.stem: Cholesterol:

options.label: A
options.text: can be absorbed from the gut by intestinal lymphatics following its incorporation into chylomicrons

options.label: B
options.text: can be synthesized in the spleen

options.label: C
options.text: in the diet comes mainly from vegetable sources

options.label: D
options.text: is eliminated from the body mainly by metabolic degradation

options.label: E
options.text: is a precursor of adrenal medulla hormones

questions.why: Dietary cholesterol is packaged into chylomicrons and absorbed via the lymphatics.

notes.B: Liver and gut.
notes.C: Animal sources.
notes.D: As bile salts and cholesterol in bile.
notes.E: Medullary hormones come from tyrosine.

questions.stem: Impaired intestinal absorption of:

options.label: A
options.text: iron occurs frequently following removal of most of the stomach

options.label: B
options.text: iodine leads to a reduction in size of the thyroid gland

options.label: C
options.text: water occurs in infants who cannot digest lipids

options.label: D
options.text: calcium is typical after removal of the colon

options.label: E
options.text: bile salts may occur following resection of the stomach

questions.why: Loss of gastric acid after major gastric resection impairs release and solubilisation of dietary non-haem iron. Altered transit or bypass of the proximal small bowel can further limit iron uptake.

notes.B: Iodine deficiency can increase stimulation of the thyroid by TSH and cause goitre. A smaller thyroid is not the usual consequence.
notes.C: Poor lipid digestion can cause steatorrhoea. Water absorption is not generally dependent on complete digestion of dietary fat.
notes.D: Regulated calcium absorption occurs chiefly in the small intestine. Removing the colon does not remove the main calcium absorption site.
notes.E: Most bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum. Gastric resection does not directly remove that transport site.

questions.stem: Complications that may arise after total gastrectomy include:

options.label: A
options.text: depletion of vitamin B12 stores in the liver

options.label: B
options.text: malabsorption of fat due to rapid intestinal transit

options.label: C
options.text: impaired defaecation due to loss of the gastric reflex

questions.why: Total gastrectomy removes the source of intrinsic factor, so vitamin B12 stores can eventually become depleted. Rapid transit and poor coordination of the meal with bile and pancreatic enzymes can also impair fat absorption.

notes.A: Parietal cells supply intrinsic factor for normal ileal B12 uptake. Without replacement, hepatic reserves can decline over time.
notes.B: Rapid delivery and poor mixing of a meal after gastrectomy can reduce the time and conditions needed for effective lipid digestion.
notes.C: Defaecation is coordinated by rectal, enteric and sacral mechanisms. Removing the stomach does not abolish this reflex.
notes.D: Protein digestion can continue through pancreatic and intestinal enzymes even though gastric pepsin digestion is lost.

questions.stem: Severe diarrhoea causes a decrease in:
questions.why: Severe diarrhoea causes faecal losses of potassium, water and salts. This can lower total body potassium and contract extracellular fluid volume, even when the measured serum potassium is affected by other factors.

notes.A: Potassium lost through large volumes of stool can decrease total body potassium and cause hypokalaemia.
notes.B: Volume depletion generally increases antidiuretic hormone release. This promotes water retention by the kidney.
notes.C: Water and sodium losses contract extracellular volume, including the circulating plasma volume.
notes.D: Sympathetic vasoconstriction usually increases peripheral resistance as a compensatory response to hypovolaemia.

questions.stem: Surgical removal of 90% of the small intestine may cause an increase in:

options.label: A
options.text: the fat content of the stools

questions.why: Extensive small-intestinal resection reduces absorptive surface and can disrupt bile-salt recycling. The resulting malabsorption can increase faecal fat and cause steatorrhoea.

notes.B: Osteomalacia is defective bone mineralisation. Malabsorption of calcium or vitamin D can decrease mineralisation over time.
notes.C: Poor absorption and high stool losses can decrease extracellular fluid volume unless fluids and electrolytes are replaced.
notes.D: Iron, folate or B12 deficiency may cause anaemia after extensive resection, depending on the segment lost and nutritional support.
notes.E: Malabsorption reduces nutrient and energy uptake and can cause weight loss rather than an increase in body weight.

questions.stem: Constipation is a recognized consequence of:

options.label: B
options.text: abnormality of the autonomic nerve supply to the esophagus

options.label: C
options.text: a diet that leaves little unabsorbed residue in the gut

options.label: D
options.text: over-activity of the thyroid gland as in thyrotoxicosis

questions.why: Low-residue diets can decrease stool bulk and contribute to constipation. Psychological stress can also alter gut motility and bowel habits. The effect of stress varies among individuals.

notes.A: Stress can affect colonic motor activity and toileting behaviour. In some people these changes contribute to constipation.
notes.B: Autonomic dysfunction confined to the oesophagus would chiefly alter swallowing or oesophageal transit. Constipation involves colonic or anorectal function.
notes.C: A low-residue diet can decrease stool bulk and reduce the stimulus for colonic propulsion.
notes.D: Thyrotoxicosis often increases bowel frequency. Constipation is more characteristic of hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: Absorption of glucose by intestinal mucosal cells:

options.label: A
options.text: relies on a carrier mechanism in the cell membrane

options.label: B
options.text: is blocked not by the same agents that block renal reabsorption of glucose

options.label: C
options.text: is enhanced by blockade of active sodium transport in the cells

options.label: D
options.text: takes place mainly in the ileum

options.label: E
options.text: does not involve the same carriers that are used for the absorption of galactose

questions.why: Apical SGLT1 carries glucose and galactose into intestinal mucosal cells with sodium. The basolateral sodium–potassium pump sustains the sodium gradient, and GLUT2 commonly carries glucose out toward the blood.

notes.B: The intestine and kidney share sodium–glucose transporter mechanisms. Phlorizin can inhibit both, although newer drugs may be selective for renal SGLT2.
notes.C: Inhibiting the sodium–potassium pump weakens the driving sodium gradient and decreases secondary active glucose entry.
notes.D: Most dietary glucose is absorbed in the proximal small intestine, especially the jejunum. The ileum can absorb glucose but is not the principal region.
notes.E: Glucose and galactose share the apical carrier SGLT1. Fructose uses a distinct entry route through GLUT5.

questions.stem: Iron is absorbed in:
questions.why: Iron is primarily absorbed in the duodenum.

notes.A: Little absorption.
notes.C: Less.
notes.D: Less.
notes.E: None.

questions.stem: In infants, defecation often follows a meal. The cause of colonic contractions in this situation is:
questions.why: A meal can trigger the gastrocolic reflex. Gastric filling and meal-related signals increase colonic motor activity, which can move stool toward the rectum and prompt defaecation soon after feeding.

notes.A: The gastroileal reflex increases ileal propulsion and promotes movement into the caecum. The question asks about colonic contractions.
notes.B: Cholecystokinin responds to nutrients and has several digestive actions. The coordinated post-meal increase in colonic activity is called the gastrocolic reflex.
notes.D: Enterogastric feedback from the small intestine can slow gastric emptying. It does not name the colonic response to feeding.
notes.E: Gastrin typically increases during a meal. A fall in gastrin does not explain the characteristic post-feeding colonic contractions.

questions.stem: Man is unable to digest:
questions.why: Humans lack digestive cellulase to hydrolyse the beta-1,4 linkages of cellulose. Cellulose therefore passes through the small intestine as fibre, although gut microbes can partly ferment some of it.

notes.A: Digestible dextrins produced from starch can be broken down by brush-border alpha-glucosidases, including enzymes that act at branch points.
notes.B: Glucose is already a monosaccharide and can be absorbed without being digested into a smaller carbohydrate.
