notes.D: Glycogen has alpha linkages that human amylases and brush-border enzymes can digest to glucose.
notes.E: Maltase activity is present at the small-intestinal brush border, where it converts maltose into two glucose molecules.

questions.stem: Steatorrhoea may be caused by all factors except:
questions.why: Haemolytic jaundice results from increased breakdown of red blood cells and bilirubin production. Isolated haemolysis does not typically impair delivery of bile salts or pancreatic lipase, and it does not usually cause steatorrhoea.

notes.A: Pancreatectomy decreases the supply of pancreatic lipase needed for normal triglyceride digestion and can cause fatty stools.
notes.B: A gastrinoma can produce enough acid to inactivate pancreatic lipase and impair bile-salt function in the small intestine.
notes.C: Extensive distal ileal resection prevents bile-salt recovery and can deplete the pool needed for normal lipid absorption.
notes.E: Coeliac disease damages the small-intestinal mucosa and can reduce lipid absorption enough to cause steatorrhoea.

questions.stem: In which of the following is absorption of water greatest:
questions.why: The jejunum normally absorbs a large share of the fluid entering the gastrointestinal tract. Sodium and nutrient uptake create osmotic gradients that draw water across the jejunal epithelium. The colon reclaims much of the smaller volume that reaches it.

notes.A: The colon absorbs water and sodium from the remaining contents. Under usual conditions, less water reaches it than is absorbed proximally.
notes.C: The duodenum can absorb water, but it also receives pancreatic and biliary fluid and has a much shorter absorptive length than the jejunum.
notes.D: The stomach stores and mixes fluid before emptying. Its role in net water uptake is small compared with the small intestine.
notes.E: Oral mucosa can absorb certain substances, but the mouth is not a major site for absorption of ingested water.

questions.stem: Vit. D is essential for normal:
questions.why: Calcitriol, the active form of vitamin D, promotes normal intestinal calcium absorption. It increases expression of proteins that allow calcium to cross the epithelium, especially when dietary calcium is limited.

notes.A: Dietary fat absorption requires adequate bile salts, pancreatic enzymes and intestinal surface. Vitamin D itself is carried with absorbed fat.
notes.C: Antidiuretic hormone release responds chiefly to plasma osmolality and effective circulating volume. It does not depend on vitamin D for its usual regulation.
notes.D: Protein absorption depends on proteolysis and transport of amino acids and small peptides. It is not the classic vitamin D-dependent process.
notes.E: Glucose absorption relies principally on apical sodium–glucose cotransport. Calcitriol chiefly regulates calcium and phosphate handling.

questions.stem: The mass movements are characteristic of the:
questions.why: Mass movements are powerful propagated contractions of the large intestine. They move contents over a long colonic segment toward the rectum and can occur in response to a meal.

notes.B: The ileum uses segmentation and peristalsis to mix and propel small-intestinal contents. Colonic mass movements are a different pattern.
notes.C: The duodenum mixes chyme with pancreatic juice and bile while regulating its delivery downstream. Mass movements describe colonic propulsion.
notes.D: The stomach grinds and propels chyme with antral peristalsis. Its emptying is regulated at the pylorus.
notes.E: The oesophagus uses peristaltic waves to move a swallowed bolus to the stomach. Long colonic mass movements serve stool transport.

questions.stem: The proteins are resorbed in the form of:
questions.why: Dietary protein is digested to free amino acids and small peptides. Enterocytes take up dipeptides and tripeptides through PepT1 and usually hydrolyse them intracellularly, so amino acids enter portal blood.

notes.A: Dipeptides are normal absorptive substrates, but larger polypeptides generally require further hydrolysis before uptake.
notes.C: Pepsinogen is a human enzyme precursor secreted into the stomach. It is not a normal absorbed product of dietary protein.
notes.D: Chylomicrons carry absorbed lipids in lymph. Products of dietary protein digestion mainly enter portal blood as amino acids.
notes.E: Luminal proteases digest dietary proteins. Intact digestive enzymes are not a main route of nutritional protein absorption.

questions.stem: The carbohydrates are resorbed as:
questions.why: Digestible carbohydrates are converted to monosaccharides before normal intestinal absorption. Glucose and galactose use sodium-coupled SGLT1 at the apical membrane, while fructose enters principally through GLUT5.

notes.A: Disaccharides are cleaved by brush-border enzymes. The resulting monosaccharides are the normal absorptive substrates.
notes.B: Glucose is absorbed, but dietary glycogen is too large for normal uptake and requires digestion to glucose.
notes.C: Glycosaminoglycans are polymers made of repeating sugar units. They are not the usual products absorbed from dietary carbohydrate.
notes.D: Glycogen is a glucose polymer. Digestive enzymes hydrolyse it before its glucose units are taken up.

questions.stem: The fats are resorbed as:

options.label: A
options.text: glycerol, free fatty acids and cholesterol

questions.why: Fats are absorbed as monoglycerides, free fatty acids, and cholesterol.

notes.B: Must be split.
notes.C: Lipases are enzymes.
notes.D: Incomplete.
notes.E: Only A is correct.

questions.stem: The secretion of K+ is in the:
questions.why: Potassium is primarily secreted into the colon (regulated by aldosterone).

notes.A: No K+ secretion.
notes.B: No K+ secretion.
notes.C: Absorbs.
notes.D: Absorbs.

questions.stem: The propulsive peristalsis of the small intestine:

options.label: C
options.text: results from smooth muscle contractions behind and in front of the zone of irritation

options.label: D
options.text: results from smooth muscles' contraction behind the zone of irritation and relaxation in front of it

options.label: E
options.text: results from smooth muscles relaxation along the small intestine

questions.why: Intestinal distension evokes an enteric peristaltic reflex. Circular muscle contracts on the oral side of the bolus and relaxes on the aboral side, producing a pressure difference that propels the contents distally.

notes.A: Segmentation mainly mixes intestinal contents. Propulsive peristalsis produces net movement away from the oral side.
notes.B: The enteric nervous system can coordinate the local reflex. The central nervous system can modulate it but does not have to generate each wave.
notes.C: The aboral segment is relaxed as the oral segment contracts. Contraction on both sides would impede the usual propulsion pattern.
notes.E: Coordinated contraction contributes the force behind the bolus. Relaxation throughout the segment would not provide this propulsive pressure.

questions.stem: Steatorrhea is caused by:

options.label: C
options.text: stoppage of bile flow into the duodenum

options.label: D
options.text: the breakdown and reabsorption of fats are disturbed

questions.why: Steatorrhoea is excess fat in stool caused by impaired fat digestion or absorption. Loss of bile delivery can impair mixed-micelle formation, and deficiencies of pancreatic enzymes or intestinal absorption can also produce fatty stools.

notes.A: Low dietary fat decreases the lipid load delivered to the bowel. Steatorrhoea represents abnormal loss of fat from the available load.
notes.B: Missing bile pigments can make stools pale in cholestasis, but pigment loss itself is not what prevents intestinal fat absorption.
notes.C: Obstructed bile flow deprives the duodenum of bile salts needed for efficient mixed-micelle formation and lipid uptake.
notes.D: Impaired hydrolysis leaves fat unprocessed, while impaired mucosal absorption leaves digestion products in the intestine. Either can increase stool fat.

questions.stem: The segment movements of the small intestine are carried out by:

options.label: C
options.text: ring like contraction, when the segment in front relaxes

questions.why: Segmentation is produced mainly by local contractions of the circular smooth muscle layer. Alternating constrictions divide and recombine the luminal contents, improving mixing with digestive secretions and contact with the mucosa.

notes.B: Longitudinal muscle shortens the bowel wall. The narrow rings characteristic of segmentation are generated chiefly by circular muscle.
notes.C: A coordinated contraction behind a bolus and relaxation ahead describes propulsive peristalsis. Segmentation mainly alternates local constrictions.
notes.D: The characteristic segmenting constrictions come principally from circular muscle. Longitudinal shortening is not the defining mechanism.
notes.E: This group adds longitudinal muscle and a leading relaxation pattern. Neither is the defining mechanism for the segmenting constriction.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements concerning energy storage in the body is true?

options.label: A
options.text: most is stored in the form of ATP

options.label: B
options.text: most is stored in the form of glucose

options.label: C
options.text: most is stored in the form of fat

options.label: D
options.text: most is stored in the form of protein

options.label: E
options.text: most is stored in the form of DNA

questions.why: Adipose triglyceride is the largest energy reserve in a typical human body. Fat is energy dense and is stored with little associated water. Glycogen supplies a smaller reserve that can be mobilised quickly.

notes.A: ATP is the immediate energy currency for cells. The standing ATP pool is small and continually regenerated.
notes.B: Free glucose in blood is a relatively small pool, and the amount stored as glycogen is limited compared with adipose triglyceride.
notes.D: Body proteins can be catabolised for energy in some conditions, but they mainly serve structural and functional roles rather than dedicated energy storage.
notes.E: DNA stores genetic information and is not a significant fuel depot.

questions.stem: The main source of energy in a typical human diet is:
questions.why: Carbohydrate normally provides the largest share of energy in a mixed human diet. Digestible starches and sugars supply monosaccharides that can be oxidised or stored, although the proportion varies with diet.

notes.A: Protein can supply energy but is also needed for amino acids. It usually provides a smaller share of energy than carbohydrate in a mixed diet.
notes.B: Vitamins support metabolic reactions, often as coenzyme precursors. They do not provide appreciable dietary energy.
notes.C: Dietary nucleic acids can be digested, but they are not a major source of dietary energy.
notes.E: Lipids provide more energy per gram than carbohydrates. The question concerns total intake in a typical diet, which depends on how much is eaten.

questions.stem: Which of the following organs or tissues is most dependent upon a constant blood supply of glucose?
questions.why: Under ordinary fed conditions, the brain depends heavily on glucose delivered by blood and has limited energy reserves. In prolonged fasting, ketone bodies replace part of its glucose requirement, but some glucose is still needed.

notes.A: The liver stores glycogen, can release glucose into the blood and can meet much of its own energy demand through fatty acid oxidation.
notes.C: Adipose tissue can use glucose, but its principal role is storing and releasing metabolic fuel. It is less immediately dependent on circulating glucose than the brain.
notes.D: Skeletal muscle has glycogen and can oxidise fatty acids as well as glucose, depending on activity and nutritional state.
notes.E: The heart normally obtains much of its energy from fatty acids and can also use lactate, ketones and glucose.

questions.stem: The hormones regulating carbohydrate metabolism (synthesis, catabolism) are:

options.label: B
options.text: insulin, glucagon, catecholamines, growth hormone, glucocorticoids (ACTH), T3 and T4 (TTH)

questions.why: Insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage, whereas glucagon and catecholamines support glucose availability during fasting or stress. Growth hormone, glucocorticoids and thyroid hormones also influence glucose turnover. ACTH and TSH regulate relevant endocrine glands upstream.

notes.A: Sex steroids can affect substrate metabolism, but this group omits the main opposing regulators of circulating glucose.
notes.C: Somatostatin can alter insulin and glucagon release. Gastrin, histamine and the other listed mediators do not form the main systemic glucose-regulating group.
notes.D: Glucagon and catecholamines are important counter-regulators, but this group omits insulin, the main hormone that lowers blood glucose after meals.
notes.E: Catecholamines, glucagon and growth hormone can affect glucose, but the group leaves out insulin and the major contribution of glucocorticoids.

questions.stem: The hormones that increase significantly the basic metabolic rate are:
questions.why: Thyroid hormones (T3, T4) are the primary regulators of BMR, but catecholamines and glucocorticoids also increase it.

notes.A: Insulin has little effect.
notes.B: Minor.
notes.C: Small effect.
notes.E: Insulin has little effect.

questions.stem: Glucose enters the blood stream via:

options.label: C
options.text: enterocytes' absorption, liver glycogen catabolism, hepatocytes and kidneys gluconeogenesis, renal proximal tubule epitheliocytes

options.label: D
options.text: degradation of glycogen in the skeletal muscles

questions.why: Blood glucose is maintained by intestinal absorption, hepatic glycogenolysis, and renal/hepatic gluconeogenesis.

notes.A: Not absorbed in the mouth.
notes.B: Muscle cannot release glucose.
notes.D: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase.
notes.E: True, but incomplete.

questions.stem: The basal metabolic rate is the energy consumption of the body under the following conditions:

options.label: A
options.text: adequate intake of vitamins regulating the intermediate processes of metabolism of the various substances

options.label: B
options.text: normal function of the endocrine glands

options.label: C
options.text: physical and psychic rest, 12 hours after the last meal in a room at a temperature of 20 - 22°C

questions.why: Basal metabolic rate is measured while awake, physically and mentally resting, postabsorptive and in a thermoneutral environment. An overnight fast helps remove the effect of a recent meal. Thermoneutrality depends on clothing and measurement conditions.

notes.A: Adequate nutrition supports normal metabolism. Vitamin intake is not itself a condition that defines basal energy measurement.
notes.B: Endocrine function affects the measured value, but the basal measurement is defined by fasting, rest and a thermoneutral environment.
notes.D: Physical activity increases muscular energy use above the basal level and is excluded from the measurement.
notes.E: Sleep can lower expenditure relative to quiet wakefulness. Pregnancy and lactation alter energy needs and are not defining measurement conditions.

questions.stem: Humoral factors taking part in the calcium/ phosphorus homeostasis are:

options.label: B
options.text: parathyroid hormone, thyrocalcitonin and vitamin D3

options.label: E
options.text: antidiuretic hormone, androgens and angiotensin II

questions.why: Parathyroid hormone, calcitriol derived from vitamin D3, and calcitonin all participate in calcium regulation. Parathyroid hormone and calcitriol have major roles in adult homeostasis. FGF23 also regulates phosphate, though it is not listed.

notes.A: Parathyroid hormone is a key calcium and phosphate regulator. Thyroxine can alter bone turnover but is not the principal complementary hormone in this set.
notes.C: Calcitonin can reduce osteoclast activity. Epinephrine chiefly mediates acute sympathetic responses rather than routine calcium–phosphate balance.
notes.D: Aldosterone promotes renal sodium retention and potassium secretion. It is not a principal partner of calcitonin in calcium regulation.
notes.E: These hormones have effects on water balance, vascular tone or reproductive function. They are not the standard calcium and phosphate regulatory group.

questions.stem: The body requires amino acids to:
questions.why: Amino acids are the building blocks for synthesizing new proteins and replacing damaged ones.

notes.A: Haem and globin need more than amino acids.
notes.B: True, but so is D.
notes.C: Vague.
notes.D: True, but so is B.

questions.stem: Which of the following will catalyze the breakdown of starches?
questions.why: Salivary and pancreatic alpha-amylases hydrolyse internal alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds in starch. They release shorter carbohydrates such as maltose, maltotriose and limit dextrins for further processing at the brush border.

notes.A: Proteases hydrolyse peptide bonds in proteins. Starch contains glycosidic bonds between glucose residues.
notes.C: Lipases hydrolyse ester bonds in dietary lipids and do not break the glucose linkages in starch.
notes.D: Sucrase acts on sucrose at the intestinal brush border. Amylase acts on the internal bonds of starch polymers.
notes.E: Peptidases release amino acids or smaller peptides from protein digestion products. They do not hydrolyse starch.

questions.stem: Which molecule represents the storage form of glucose in the liver?
questions.why: Hepatocytes store glucose units as glycogen, a highly branched polysaccharide. They can break it down and release glucose into blood between meals, which helps maintain plasma glucose.

notes.B: Glucagon is a pancreatic hormone that stimulates hepatic glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis. It is not the stored carbohydrate.
notes.C: A disaccharide has two monosaccharide units. Hepatic glycogen contains many branched chains of glucose residues.
notes.D: Lactate can be used by the liver for gluconeogenesis. It is not the principal storage form of glucose.
notes.E: Carbonic acid is involved in acid–base chemistry and carbon dioxide transport, not storage of carbohydrate energy.

questions.stem: Appetite for food is increased:
questions.why: Cold exposure can increase thermoregulatory energy expenditure and can increase hunger. The effect varies with exposure and individual response. Gastric distension and cholecystokinin typically signal meal termination.

notes.A: Cholecystokinin is released in response to fat and protein digestion products and contributes to post-meal satiation.
notes.B: Calcitonin acts mainly in calcium and bone physiology. It is not a usual physiological trigger for hunger.
notes.C: Gastric distension activates stretch signals that usually increase fullness and limit meal size.
notes.D: Denervation can disrupt fullness signals and gastric motility. It has no predictable general effect of increasing appetite.

questions.stem: The respiratory quotient (RQ):

options.label: A
options.text: is the volume of O2 consumed to the volume of CO2 produced ratio

options.label: B
options.text: depends essentially on the type of substrate being metabolized and is 1.0 when the substrate is glucose

options.label: C
options.text: is 1.0 in conditions of metabolic alcalosis

options.label: D
options.text: is between 0.9 and 1.0 in the second week of fasting

options.label: E
options.text: is above 0.8 if fats are mainly metabolized

questions.why: Respiratory quotient is carbon dioxide produced divided by oxygen consumed. Complete glucose oxidation uses six molecules of oxygen and produces six molecules of carbon dioxide, so glucose has an RQ of 1.0.

notes.A: This ratio is inverted. The numerator of the respiratory quotient is carbon dioxide production.
notes.C: Acid–base disturbances can alter measured gas exchange at the lungs. They do not set the cellular substrate RQ to 1.0.
notes.D: Prolonged fasting increases reliance on fatty acids and ketones. The respiratory quotient generally shifts downward rather than staying near the carbohydrate value.
notes.E: Predominant fatty acid oxidation typically produces an RQ near 0.7. Values nearer or above 0.8 suggest a larger contribution from other fuels.

questions.stem: Oxygen consumption tends to increase when the:

options.label: A
options.text: concentration of oxygen in inspired air rises

options.label: C
options.text: body temperature rises and environmental temperature falls

questions.why: Oxygen consumption generally rises as tissue metabolism increases with higher body temperature. A cold environment can also increase oxygen demand through shivering and non-shivering thermogenesis when it is below the thermoneutral range.

notes.A: Higher inspired oxygen does not usually increase resting oxygen use in a healthy person. Tissue energy demand is the main determinant.
notes.B: A lower metabolic rate generally decreases oxygen consumption because less oxidative ATP production is needed.
notes.D: Warming a cold person toward thermoneutrality decreases the need for heat production. Extreme heat can raise demands through other mechanisms.
notes.E: Eating generally increases energy expenditure through the thermic effect of food. The resting postabsorptive state lacks most of that effect.

questions.stem: Brown fat is:

options.label: A
options.text: relatively more abundant in adults than in infants

options.label: B
options.text: richer in mitochondria than ordinary fat and has an extensive sympathetic innervation

options.label: C
options.text: produces less heat and more ATP than other tissues

options.label: D
options.text: stimulated to generate more heat when its parasympathetic nerve supply is stimulated

options.label: E
options.text: less important than shivering in neonatal thermoregulation

questions.why: Brown adipose cells have many mitochondria and rich sympathetic innervation. Noradrenaline can activate thermogenesis, in which UCP1 allows proton leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane and promotes heat production.

notes.A: Brown adipose tissue is especially important in newborns, although adults retain deposits that can be metabolically active.
notes.C: UCP1 decreases the coupling of oxidation to ATP synthesis, so a greater share of the energy is released as heat.
notes.D: Cold-induced brown fat thermogenesis is driven largely by sympathetic noradrenergic activity rather than parasympathetic stimulation.
notes.E: Non-shivering thermogenesis in brown fat is important in newborns because their capacity for effective shivering is limited.

questions.stem: Nitrogen balance:

options.label: A
options.text: is the relationship between the body's nitrogen intake and nitrogen loss

options.label: C
options.text: becomes more positive when dietary protein is decreased

options.label: D
options.text: becomes positive whenever a single essential amino acid is omitted from the diet

options.label: E
options.text: becomes less negative in the final stages of fatal starvation

questions.why: Nitrogen balance is nitrogen intake minus nitrogen loss. Since proteins supply most dietary nitrogen, a positive value generally reflects net protein accretion, while a negative value reflects loss of body protein.

notes.B: Healthy growing children usually have positive nitrogen balance because growing tissues retain protein.
notes.C: Reducing protein intake generally lowers nitrogen input. Unless losses decline enough to compensate, balance becomes less positive or negative.
notes.D: An essential amino acid must be supplied by the diet. Its omission limits protein synthesis and can make nitrogen balance negative.
notes.E: Protein is relatively spared during adapted fasting, but in advanced starvation protein breakdown can rise as fat stores are depleted.

questions.stem: The specific dynamic action of food:

options.label: A
options.text: is the decrease in metabolic rate that results from ingestion of food

options.label: B
options.text: persists for about an hour after a meal is ingested

options.label: C
options.text: is due to the additional energy expended in digesting and absorbing the food

options.label: D
options.text: results in about 30 per cent of the energy value of ingested protein being unavailable for other purposes

options.label: E
options.text: results in about 20 per cent of the energy value of ingested fat and carbohydrate being unavailable for other purposes

questions.why: The specific dynamic action of food is the increase in energy expenditure after eating. Protein has the greatest thermic effect, commonly about 20–30 percent of its energy, because processing amino acids and forming urea are metabolically costly.

notes.A: Energy expenditure increases after a meal because digestion, absorption and subsequent nutrient handling require energy.
notes.B: The response can last several hours. Its duration depends on meal size and composition.
notes.C: Digestion and absorption contribute, but further nutrient processing, storage and nitrogen disposal are also part of the thermic effect.
notes.E: Fat generally has a small thermic effect, and carbohydrate has an intermediate one. Their usual fractions are below that of dietary protein.

questions.stem: One gram of:

options.label: A
options.text: carbohydrate, metabolized in the body, yields more energy when oxidized in a bomb calorimeter

options.label: B
options.text: fat, metabolized in the body, yields 10 per cent more energy than 1g of carbohydrate

options.label: C
options.text: protein, metabolized in the body, yields the same energy as when oxidized in a bomb calorimeter

options.label: D
options.text: carbohydrate, metabolized in the body, yields about the same energy as 1g of protein

options.label: E
options.text: protein per kg body weight is not the adequate daily protein intake for a sedentary adult

questions.why: Metabolisable energy is approximately 4 kilocalories per gram for both dietary carbohydrate and protein. A gram of fat provides about 9 kilocalories. Gross combustion values, particularly for protein, differ from usable energy in the body.

notes.A: Most available carbohydrate yields broadly similar gross and physiological energy values. The gap is more important for protein because of nitrogenous waste.
notes.B: One gram of fat provides about 9 kilocalories, which is more than twice the energy from one gram of carbohydrate.
notes.C: A bomb calorimeter measures the full heat of protein combustion. The body excretes some energy in nitrogenous products, making the physiological yield lower.
notes.E: One gram of protein per kilogram of body weight is generally adequate for a healthy sedentary adult. Exact requirements depend on age and circumstances.

questions.stem: Free (non-esterified) fatty acids in plasma:

options.label: A
options.text: are carried in plasma mainly inside chylomicrons

options.label: C
options.text: decrease when the level of blood adrenaline rises

options.label: D
options.text: cannot be used for energy by cardiac muscle

options.label: E
options.text: are never synthesized in adipose tissue

questions.why: Non-esterified fatty acids are poorly soluble in plasma and bind to albumin for transport. They can be released from adipose triglyceride and delivered to oxidative tissues such as heart and skeletal muscle.

notes.A: Chylomicrons mainly carry esterified fatty acids in triglycerides. Albumin carries most circulating non-esterified fatty acids.
notes.C: Adrenaline can stimulate adipose lipolysis and increase release of non-esterified fatty acids, especially during stress or exercise.
notes.D: Cardiac muscle readily oxidises fatty acids and commonly uses them as an important aerobic fuel.
notes.E: Adipocytes can make fatty acids and can release free fatty acids by hydrolysing stored triglycerides.

questions.stem: Fat stores in the adult:

options.label: A
options.text: make up less than 5 % of average body weight

options.label: B
options.text: Make up a smaller percentage of body weight in women than in men

options.label: C
options.text: release fatty acids when there is increased sympathetic nerve activity

options.label: D
options.text: release fatty acids when insulin is injected

options.label: E
options.text: enlarge by increasing the number of adipocytes they contain

questions.why: Sympathetic stimulation (via beta-3 receptors) stimulates lipolysis in adipose tissue.

notes.A: About 15–25%.
notes.B: Higher in women.
notes.D: Insulin INHIBITS lipolysis.
notes.E: Mainly by size (hypertrophy).

questions.stem: Metabolic rate can be estimated from measurements of:

options.label: B
options.text: the calorific value of the food consumed in the previous 24 hours

options.label: C
options.text: oxygen consumption and the respiratory quotient

options.label: D
options.text: carbon dioxide production and the respiratory quotient

questions.why: Indirect calorimetry estimates metabolic rate by measuring O2 consumption and CO2 production.

notes.A: Direct calorimetry, but not the usual estimate.
notes.B: Not accurate.
notes.C: True, but D too.
notes.D: True, but C too.

questions.stem: Carbonic anhydrase has a role to play in the formation of:

options.label: A
options.text: HCl by the parietal cells of the stomach

options.label: C
options.text: cerebrospinal fluid in the choroid plexuses

questions.why: Carbonic anhydrase accelerates formation of hydrogen ions and bicarbonate from carbon dioxide and water. In parietal cells it supports gastric acid secretion. In the choroid plexus it supports bicarbonate-dependent ion and fluid secretion into the cerebrospinal fluid.

notes.A: Hydrogen ions generated in parietal cells are delivered to the gastric lumen by the hydrogen–potassium ATPase.
notes.B: Carbaminohaemoglobin forms when carbon dioxide binds directly to amino groups on globin. That reaction is distinct from carbonic anhydrase-mediated bicarbonate formation.
notes.C: Choroid plexus ion transport uses bicarbonate and contributes to cerebrospinal fluid production. Carbonic anhydrase inhibition can decrease this secretion.
notes.D: Bile salts are derived from cholesterol in hepatocytes. Biliary bicarbonate secretion is a separate process.

questions.stem: The energy equivalent of oxygen (EEO) is:

options.label: A
options.text: determined by the body temperature and is the same when all the substances are oxidized

options.label: B
options.text: the amount of energy released, when one litre of O2 is utilized for the oxidation of a given substance

options.label: C
options.text: of highest value when lipids are oxidized, since they have the highest calorie content

options.label: D
options.text: the ratio of CO2 produced and O2 utilized

options.label: E
options.text: the energy, expended at rest for 24 hours

questions.why: The energy equivalent of oxygen is the energy released when one litre of oxygen is consumed during substrate oxidation. It varies with the fuel. Carbohydrate yields more energy per litre of oxygen than fat, despite fat yielding more per gram.

notes.A: The value depends mainly on the fuel being oxidised and its stoichiometry. It is not a common fixed value set by body temperature.
notes.C: Fat provides more energy per gram but requires proportionally more oxygen. Its energy yield per litre of oxygen is lower than that of carbohydrate.
notes.D: Carbon dioxide production divided by oxygen consumption gives the respiratory quotient. That ratio helps identify the appropriate caloric equivalent.
notes.E: Resting energy use over a day is an expenditure measured over time. The energy equivalent of oxygen is expressed per litre of oxygen.
